No. The error in your argument is assuming all radiation is unidirectional, which, in all fairness, is an easy assumption to make. A simple counterexample would be lasers and masers (beams, like it appears they are describing in the article) whose only losses are absorption and other minor 2nd and 3rd order scattering effects.

The Inverse Square 'law' isn't a law per se, but a description of a unidirectional propagation pattern, like what a point source might emit. It is also wrong to describe it as a 'loss', as the word is normally reserved for energy irrecoverably converted to heat, where this propagation pattern is a description of decreasing density over increasing area.

Furthermore, the only macroscale situation we know of that demonstrates this propagation pattern proper is gravity between large objects. No real antenna can radiate unidirectionally (a dipole antenna [for example] has nulls along its axis).

Also, just to be difficult, microwaves traveling in the TE or TM modes (inside a waveguide) do indeed propagate with electrons giving rise to a phenomenon called surface plasmon-polaritons - look it up.

In conclusion, everything depends. Lol the word 'law' doesn't mean the same thing in the science world as it does in the legal world.
